en.titulo: Measures of centre and of spread
en.resumo: Summarising a data set with the mean, median and mode, and measuring how far the values spread from the centre using the range and the mean deviation.
en.explicacao:
#### Two different questions about the same data set

Faced with a list of numbers, there are two questions that must not be mixed up.

The first is: **around which value do the data cluster?** That is answered by the measures of
centre, which are the mean, the median and the mode.

The second is: **how widely do the data spread around that value?** That is answered by the measures
of spread, which are the range and the mean deviation.

Two groups can have exactly the same mean and be completely different. A class where everybody
scored 7 and a class where half scored 4 and half scored 10 have the same mean, and no sensible
person would say the two classes are alike. That is why the second question matters as much as the
first.

#### Mean

The mean is the sum of the values divided by how many there are:

M = S / n

where M is the mean, S the sum of all the values and n how many values there are. It shares the
total out equally, as if everyone received the same portion.

**Example 1.** Find the mean of 4, 7, 8, 9 and 12.
The sum is S = 40 and there are n = 5 values, so M = 40 / 5 = 8.

The mean uses every piece of data, and that is both its strength and its weakness: one value far
from the pattern shifts the whole mean.

#### Median

The median is the value sitting in the middle once the data are put in order. If the number of
values is odd, it is the middle one. If it is even, it is the mean of the two central ones:

Md = (c_{1} + c_{2}) / 2

where Md is the median and c_{1} and c_{2} are the two central values.

**Example 2.** Find the median of 3, 5, 8, 9, 10 and 14.
There are 6 values, so the central ones are 8 and 9, and Md = (8 + 9) / 2 = 8.5.

Since the median only looks at position, it is not dragged around by an extreme value. That is why
the salaries of a country are usually described by the median rather than the mean.

#### Mode

The mode is the value that appears most often. A set can have one mode, more than one, or none at
all, when every value appears the same number of times. The mode is the only one of the three that
also works for data that are not numbers, such as favourite colour or means of transport.

#### Range

The range is the difference between the largest and the smallest value:

R = x_{max} - x_{min}

where R is the range, x_{max} the largest value in the set and x_{min} the smallest. It is the
simplest measure of spread, and it gives a first idea of how scattered the data are.

**Example 3.** Find the range of 4, 7, 8, 9 and 12.
The largest value is 12 and the smallest is 4, so R = 12 - 4 = 8.

Its limitation is that it uses only two numbers from the set. A single very distant value inflates
the range even when everything else is tightly grouped.

#### Mean deviation

The mean deviation looks at every piece of data. The procedure has three steps:

1. Work out the mean M.
2. For each value x, work out the distance |x - M|, always as a positive amount.
3. Work out the mean of those distances.

MD = S_{d} / n

where MD is the mean deviation, S_{d} the sum of the distances |x - M| and n how many values there
are.

**Example 4.** Find the mean deviation of 4, 7, 8, 9 and 12.
The mean is M = 8. The distances |x - 8| are 4, 1, 0, 1 and 4, which add up to S_{d} = 10. Then
MD = 10 / 5 = 2.

The reading is direct: on average, each value in the set sits 2 units away from the centre. The
smaller the mean deviation, the more uniform the set.

The distances step has to use positive amounts. If the differences are added with their signs, the
result is always zero, because the mean balances what lies above it against what lies below.

#### Common mistakes

**Forgetting to sort before finding the median.** The median is a position, and the position only
exists after sorting.

**Dividing by the wrong count.** In a mean weighted by frequencies, the divisor is the total number
of occurrences, not the number of distinct values.

**Adding signed differences in the mean deviation.** The total comes to zero and the calculation is
lost.

**Confusing the mode with the largest value.** The mode is the most frequent value, and it may well
be the smallest of them all.

**Assuming that equal means imply similar sets.** Two lists with the same mean can have very
different spreads, and it is the spread that says whether summarising by the mean is trustworthy.

Find the mode of the set 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 3 and 8.

Find the mean deviation of the set 4, 7, 8, 9 and 12.

exercicios.resposta: The mean is 5000 reais and the median is 2400 reais. The median describes it better, because the highest salary pulls the mean upwards and no employee earns anywhere near 5000 reais.

exercicios.enunciado: In a test, the mark 5 appeared 2 times, the mark 6 appeared 3 times, the mark 7 appeared 4 times and the mark 8 appeared 1 time. Find the class mean.
exercicios.resposta: 6.4. The marks add up to 64 and there are 10 marks in all.

exercicios.resposta: Both sets have mean 10. Set A has range 4 and mean deviation 1.2. Set B has range 16 and mean deviation 4.8. Set A is more uniform.

exercicios.enunciado: A set of four numbers has mean 15, and three of them are 10, 14 and 20. Find the fourth number.
Consider the set 4, 7, 8, 9 and 12. Add 5 to each value and say what happens to the mean, to the range and to the mean deviation. Explain why the effect is the same for any set.
exercicios.resposta: The mean goes from 8 to 13. The range stays at 8 and the mean deviation stays at 2. Adding the same amount to every value shifts the whole set without changing the distances between the values, and it is those distances that spread measures.

exercicios.enunciado: The mean of a set of 10 numbers is 7. One of the numbers is removed and the mean of the remaining 9 becomes 6. Find the number that was removed.
exercicios.resposta: 16. The sum of the 10 numbers is 70 and the sum of the remaining 9 is 54.

exercicios.enunciado: In a test, class A has 20 students and mean 7, while class B has 30 students and mean 6. Find the mean of the two classes together and explain why it is not 6.5.
exercicios.resposta: The combined mean is 6.4. The marks add up to 140 in class A and 180 in class B, which gives 320 for 50 students. The plain average of 7 and 6 would give 6.5, but the classes have different sizes and the larger class weighs more in the result.

pt.resumo: Calcular a probabilidade de dois ou mais acontecimentos em sequência, distinguindo o caso com reposição do caso sem reposição.
pt.explicacao:
#### O ponto de partida

A probabilidade de um acontecimento, num experimento em que todos os resultados são igualmente
prováveis, é a razão entre o número de casos favoráveis e o número de casos possíveis:

P = casos favoráveis / casos possíveis

onde P é a probabilidade do acontecimento. Ela vale sempre entre 0 e 1, isto é, 0 ≤ P ≤ 1, e é boa
prática deixar a resposta como fração irredutível.

Num dado comum, a probabilidade de sair um número par é 3 casos favoráveis em 6 possíveis, ou seja,
P = 3/6 = 1/2.

#### Quando os acontecimentos vêm em sequência

O tema deste material é o que acontece quando o experimento tem mais de uma etapa: duas moedas
lançadas, duas bolas retiradas de uma urna, três cartas tiradas do baralho. A regra é curta:

**A probabilidade de dois acontecimentos ocorrerem em sequência é o produto das probabilidades,
sendo que a segunda é calculada na situação deixada pela primeira.**

A segunda metade dessa frase é onde mora toda a dificuldade, e ela se resolve com uma única
pergunta: **a primeira etapa mudou alguma coisa para a segunda?**

#### Com reposição: as etapas não se afetam

Se a bola retirada volta para a urna antes da segunda retirada, a urna na segunda etapa é exatamente
a mesma da primeira. As duas etapas são **independentes**, e as duas frações têm o mesmo
denominador.

**Exemplo 1.** Duas moedas honestas são lançadas. Qual é a probabilidade de sair cara nas duas?
A primeira moeda não interfere na segunda. A probabilidade é 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

**Exemplo 2.** Uma urna tem 5 bolas vermelhas e 3 azuis. Duas bolas são retiradas em sequência, com
reposição da primeira antes da segunda. Qual é a probabilidade de as duas serem vermelhas?
Em cada retirada a probabilidade de vermelha é 5/8. O resultado é 5/8 × 5/8 = 25/64.

#### Sem reposição: a segunda etapa muda

Se a bola retirada fica fora, a urna encolhe. Na segunda retirada há uma bola a menos no total, e
uma a menos também da cor que saiu. As etapas são **dependentes**.

**Exemplo 3.** Na mesma urna de 5 bolas vermelhas e 3 azuis, duas bolas são retiradas sem reposição.
Qual é a probabilidade de as duas serem vermelhas?
A primeira tem probabilidade 5/8. Depois de sair uma vermelha, sobram 4 vermelhas em 7 bolas, então
a segunda tem probabilidade 4/7. O produto é 5/8 × 4/7 = 20/56, que simplifica para 5/14.

Compare com o caso anterior: 25/64 contra 5/14. Tirar sem reposição deixa menos bolas vermelhas
disponíveis, e a probabilidade de duas vermelhas cai.

Por isso o enunciado precisa sempre dizer se há reposição, e ler essa palavra é o primeiro passo da
resolução.

#### Pelo menos um: use o complementar

Quando a pergunta é "qual a probabilidade de sair pelo menos um", contar os casos favoráveis dá
trabalho, porque eles são muitos. O caminho curto é calcular a probabilidade do contrário, que é
"nenhum", e subtrair de 1.

**Exemplo 4.** Três moedas honestas são lançadas. Qual é a probabilidade de sair pelo menos uma
cara?
O contrário de pelo menos uma cara é nenhuma cara, isto é, coroa nas três, com probabilidade
1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8. Logo a resposta é 1 - 1/8 = 7/8.

#### A árvore de possibilidades

Desenhar a árvore ajuda quando há mais de um caminho favorável. Cada galho recebe a probabilidade
daquela etapa, cada caminho completo vale o produto dos galhos, e caminhos diferentes que levam ao
mesmo resultado são somados.

Vale guardar a regra de leitura: **e multiplica, ou soma**. Sair vermelha e depois azul é produto.
Sair vermelha e depois azul ou azul e depois vermelha é soma de dois produtos.

#### Erros comuns

**Somar quando deveria multiplicar.** Em etapas sucessivas, o conectivo é o "e", e o "e" multiplica.
Somar probabilidades de etapas seguidas costuma dar resultado maior que 1, o que é impossível.

**Manter o denominador na retirada sem reposição.** Se saiu uma bola e ela não voltou, a segunda
fração tem um total menor.

**Esquecer de tirar também do numerador.** Ao retirar uma bola vermelha sem reposição, diminui o
total e diminui a quantidade de vermelhas.

**Ignorar a ordem quando ela importa.** Primeira vermelha e segunda azul é um caso. Se o enunciado
aceita as duas ordens, os dois produtos precisam ser somados.

**Deixar a resposta sem simplificar.** A fração irredutível é a forma esperada, e simplificar
costuma revelar erro de conta.

exercicios.resposta: 20/90, que simplifica para 2/9. Há 5 fichas pares entre as 10.

exercicios.resposta: 8/15. O caso contrário é não sair amarela nenhuma, que tem probabilidade 7/15.

Uma urna contém 3 bolas pretas e n bolas brancas. Duas bolas são retiradas sem reposição, e a probabilidade de as duas serem pretas vale 1/15. Determine n.
exercicios.resposta: n = 7. A condição leva a (3 + n) · (2 + n) = 90, e a única raiz positiva é 7.

en.resumo: Working out the probability of two or more events in sequence, telling the case with replacement apart from the case without replacement.
en.explicacao:
#### The starting point

The probability of an event, in an experiment where all outcomes are equally likely, is the ratio
between the number of favourable cases and the number of possible cases:

P = favourable cases / possible cases

where P is the probability of the event. It always lies between 0 and 1, that is, 0 ≤ P ≤ 1, and it
is good practice to leave the answer as a fraction in lowest terms.

On a standard die, the probability of getting an even number is 3 favourable cases out of 6
possible, that is, P = 3/6 = 1/2.

#### When events come in sequence

The subject of this material is what happens when the experiment has more than one stage: two coins
tossed, two balls drawn from an urn, three cards taken from a deck. The rule is short:

**The probability of two events happening in sequence is the product of the probabilities, where the
second one is worked out in the situation left behind by the first.**

The second half of that sentence is where all the difficulty lives, and it is settled by a single
question: **did the first stage change anything for the second?**

#### With replacement: the stages do not affect each other

If the ball drawn goes back into the urn before the second draw, the urn at the second stage is
exactly the one from the first. The two stages are **independent**, and both fractions have the same
denominator.

**Example 1.** Two fair coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting heads on both?
The first coin does not interfere with the second. The probability is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

**Example 2.** An urn holds 5 red balls and 3 blue ones. Two balls are drawn in sequence, with the
first put back before the second. What is the probability that both are red?
At each draw the probability of red is 5/8. The result is 5/8 × 5/8 = 25/64.

#### Without replacement: the second stage changes

If the ball drawn stays out, the urn shrinks. At the second draw there is one ball fewer in the
total, and one fewer of the colour that came out as well. The stages are **dependent**.

**Example 3.** In the same urn with 5 red balls and 3 blue ones, two balls are drawn without
replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
The first has probability 5/8. Once a red ball is out, 4 red balls remain among 7 balls, so the
second has probability 4/7. The product is 5/8 × 4/7 = 20/56, which simplifies to 5/14.

Compare this with the previous case: 25/64 against 5/14. Drawing without replacement leaves fewer
red balls available, and the probability of two reds falls.

That is why the question must always state whether there is replacement, and reading that word is
the first step of the solution.

#### At least one: use the complement

When the question is "what is the probability of at least one", counting the favourable cases is
laborious, because there are many of them. The short route is to work out the probability of the
opposite, which is "none", and subtract it from 1.

**Example 4.** Three fair coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting at least one head?
The opposite of at least one head is no heads at all, that is, tails three times, with probability
1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8. So the answer is 1 - 1/8 = 7/8.

#### The probability tree

Drawing the tree helps when there is more than one favourable path. Each branch carries the
probability of that stage, each complete path is worth the product of its branches, and different
paths leading to the same outcome are added together.

The reading rule is worth keeping: **and multiplies, or adds**. Getting red and then blue is a
product. Getting red and then blue, or blue and then red, is a sum of two products.

#### Common mistakes

**Adding when you should multiply.** In successive stages the connective is "and", and "and"
multiplies. Adding the probabilities of consecutive stages usually gives a result larger than 1,
which is impossible.

**Keeping the denominator in a draw without replacement.** If a ball came out and did not go back,
the second fraction has a smaller total.

**Forgetting to take one off the numerator too.** Drawing a red ball without replacement lowers the
total and lowers the number of reds.

**Ignoring order when it matters.** First red and second blue is one case. If the question accepts
both orders, the two products have to be added.

**Leaving the answer unsimplified.** A fraction in lowest terms is the expected form, and
simplifying often reveals an arithmetic slip.

exercicios.enunciado: A standard six faced die is rolled once. What is the probability of getting the number 5?
Two fair coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting heads on both?
An urn holds 5 red balls and 3 blue balls. One ball is drawn at random. What is the probability that it is red?
Two standard dice are rolled. What is the probability of getting the number 6 on both?
A card is drawn at random from a deck of 52 cards, of which 13 are hearts. What is the probability that the card is a heart?
exercicios.resposta: 13/52, which simplifies to 1/4.

exercicios.enunciado: An urn holds 5 red balls and 3 blue balls. Two balls are drawn in sequence, with the first put back before the second. What is the probability that both are red?
exercicios.resposta: 25/64. With replacement the urn goes back to its original state, and the two fractions are equal.

exercicios.enunciado: An urn holds 5 red balls and 3 blue balls. Two balls are drawn in sequence, without replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
exercicios.resposta: 20/56, which simplifies to 5/14. At the second draw 4 red balls remain among 7 balls.

exercicios.enunciado: Three fair coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting at least one head?
exercicios.resposta: 7/8. The opposite case is getting no heads at all, whose probability is 1/8.

exercicios.enunciado: A box holds 4 blue pens and 6 black pens. Two pens are drawn in sequence, without replacement. What is the probability that both are black?
exercicios.resposta: 30/90, which simplifies to 1/3.

exercicios.enunciado: Two standard dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum of the results is 7?
exercicios.resposta: 6/36, which simplifies to 1/6.

exercicios.enunciado: An urn holds 5 red balls and 3 blue balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that the first is red and the second is blue, in that order?
A bag contains 10 counters numbered from 1 to 10. Two counters are drawn in sequence, without replacement. What is the probability that both carry an even number?
exercicios.resposta: 20/90, which simplifies to 2/9. There are 5 even counters among the 10.

exercicios.enunciado: A standard die is rolled twice. What is the probability of not getting the number 6 on either of the two rolls?

An urn holds 6 white balls and 4 black balls. Work out the probability of drawing two white balls with replacement, work out the probability of drawing two white balls without replacement, and say which of the two situations is more likely.
exercicios.resposta: With replacement the probability is 9/25 and without replacement it is 1/3. Since 9/25 = 0.36 and 1/3 is worth about 0.333, the case with replacement is the more likely one.

exercicios.enunciado: An urn holds 7 green balls and 3 yellow balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. What is the probability of getting at least one yellow ball?
exercicios.resposta: 8/15. The opposite case is getting no yellow ball at all, whose probability is 7/15.

exercicios.enunciado: A box holds 5 blue balls and 5 red balls. Three balls are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that all three are blue?
An urn contains 3 black balls and n white balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement, and the probability that both are black is 1/15. Find n.
exercicios.resposta: n = 7. The condition leads to (3 + n) · (2 + n) = 90, and the only positive root is 7.

exercicios.enunciado: A student answers each question of a test correctly with probability 80%, independently from one question to the next. In a test with 4 questions, what is the probability that he gets the first three right and the last one wrong?
